claim: Advances in biological engineering are likely to have substantial impacts on global society.
source: Advances in biological engineering are likely to have substantial impacts on global society.
evidence: This is a stated premise of the study in the abstract, representing the authors' assessment based on their expertise.

claim: Recent advances in synthetic biology, notably in gene-editing techniques, have substantially increased our capabilities for biological engineering.
source: Recent advances in synthetic biology, notably in gene-editing techniques, have substantially increased our capabilities for biological engineering, as have advances in areas such as information technology and robotics.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact about recent technological progress in the field.

claim: Very few conservation practitioners had heard of synthetic biology in 2012.
source: For example, after identifying that very few conservation practitioners had even heard of synthetic biology in 2012, scientists from both disciplines convened in 2013 to explore how synthetic biology and conservation would shape the future of nature (Redford et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Redford et al., 2013.

claim: A 2014 horizon scan flagged the use of gene-editing to control invasive species or disease vectors.
source: In the same year, a horizon scan of emerging issues of interest to the conservation community (Sutherland et al., 2014) flagged the use of gene-editing to control invasive species or disease vectors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sutherland et al., 2014.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 approaches to controlling disease-carrying mosquitos have rapidly gained traction since 2013.
source: Since then, CRISPR/Cas9 approaches to controlling disease-carrying mosquitos (Adelman and Tu, 2016) and invasive species (Esvelt et al., 2014) have rapidly gained traction.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Adelman and Tu, 2016 and Esvelt et al., 2014.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 approaches to controlling invasive species have rapidly gained traction since 2013.
source: Since then, CRISPR/Cas9 approaches to controlling disease-carrying mosquitos (Adelman and Tu, 2016) and invasive species (Esvelt et al., 2014) have rapidly gained traction.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Adelman and Tu, 2016 and Esvelt et al., 2014.

claim: Outputs of horizon scanning activities in Antarctic science have underpinned roadmaps outlining enabling technologies, access, logistics, infrastructure, and international cooperation.
source: Outputs of similarly structured horizon scanning activities in Antarctic science (Kennicutt et al., 2014) have underpinned roadmaps outlining the enabling technologies, access to the region, logistics and infrastructure, and international cooperation (Kennicutt et al., 2016) required to "deliver the science".
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kennicutt et al., 2014 and 2016.

claim: Antarctic science horizon scanning outputs have been used to guide investment of national programs.
source: These have since been used to guide investment of national programs (National Academies, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to National Academies, 2015.

claim: The Natural Environment Research Council in the UK has drawn on annual horizon scans in conservation to inform their strategic planning.
source: Similarly, the Natural Environment Research Council in the UK has drawn on annual horizon scans in conservation (see, for example, Sutherland et al., 2014) to inform their strategic planning.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sutherland et al., 2014.

claim: The horizon scan comprised 27 participants with diverse expertise in biological engineering.
source: The horizon scan comprised a set of participants blending academic, industry, innovation, security, and policy expertise related to biological engineering, with a range of backgrounds in natural sciences, engineering, social sciences, and humanities. Each of the 27 participants (the authors minus facilitators) submitted short summaries of 2-5 'issues'
evidence: This is a direct description of the study methodology.

claim: A total of 70 issue summaries were submitted after merging duplicates.
source: After merging duplicates, a total of 70 issue summaries were anonymized and circulated to all participants
evidence: This is a direct report of the data collection process.

claim: The inter-rater concordance of first round scores was substantial and statistically highly significant (Kendall's W=0.150, p-value < 10−15).
source: Our analysis of first round data indicates that while there was considerable diversity in the raw scores provided by individual participants, the inter-rater concordance was substantial and statistically highly significant (Kendall's W=0.150, p-value < 10−15).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the collected data.

claim: The rank correlation between individual participants ranged between 0.002 and 0.463, with a median of 0.112.
source: The rank correlation between individual participants ranged between 0.002 and 0.463, with a median of 0.112 (Spearman's rho).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the collected data.

claim: Biology-based methods of carbon capture include using bioreactors to catalyse the production of fuels in fermentation bioreactors.
source: Biology-based methods of carbon capture include using bioreactors to catalyse the production of fuels in fermentation bioreactors (Patent 20150247171, Lanzatech, NZ)
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to a patent.

claim: Artificial photosynthesis uses solar energy to drive an electrochemical reduction of CO2 to methanol.
source: or creating 'artificial photosynthesis' that uses solar energy to drive an electrochemical reduction of CO2 to methanol (Ager, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ager, 2016.

claim: A 'bionic leaf' using Ralstonia eutropha can produce biomass and liquid fusel alcohols at carbon reduction efficiencies that exceed the rate achieved by photosynthesis in terrestrial plants.
source: For example, a 'bionic leaf' in which inorganic catalysts are interfaced with the bacterium Ralstonia eutropha is able to produce biomass and liquid fusel alcohols at carbon reduction efficiencies that exceed the rate achieved by photosynthesis in terrestrial plants (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2016.

claim: A hybrid nanowire-bacterial system for fixing CO2 at high efficiencies has been reported.
source: A hybrid nanowire-bacterial system for fixing CO2 at high efficiencies has also been reported (Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2015.

claim: The world population is expected to exceed nine billion people in 2050.
source: In order to feed an expected world population of more than nine billion people in 2050, agricultural productivity will need to more than double in the face of shrinking croplands (Alexandratos and Bruinsma, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Alexandratos and Bruinsma, 2012.

claim: Agricultural productivity will need to more than double by 2050 to feed the expected world population.
source: In order to feed an expected world population of more than nine billion people in 2050, agricultural productivity will need to more than double in the face of shrinking croplands (Alexandratos and Bruinsma, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Alexandratos and Bruinsma, 2012.

claim: Growth in agricultural productivity of the most important food crops has been stagnating.
source: Instead, growth in agricultural productivity of the most important food crops has been stagnating (Ray et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ray et al., 2012.

claim: The large gains in yield of the Green Revolution were primarily driven by increases in biomass partition into grain (harvest index).
source: The large gains in yield of the Green Revolution were primarily driven by increases in biomass partition into grain (harvest index), which is now near the theoretical upper limit.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about agricultural history.

claim: Harvest index is now near the theoretical upper limit.
source: The large gains in yield of the Green Revolution were primarily driven by increases in biomass partition into grain (harvest index), which is now near the theoretical upper limit.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about agricultural limits.

claim: Synthetic biology is providing techniques to enhance photosynthesis.
source: A promising approach to significantly boosting crop yields is to enhance photosynthesis. This has been discussed for some time, but synthetic biology is now providing the techniques to achieve it (Furbank et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Furbank et al., 2015.

claim: An attempt is underway to increase yield potential by engineering C4 photosynthesis into rice.
source: For example, an attempt is underway to increase yield potential by engineering a more efficient type of photosynthesis known as C4 into rice (http://photosynthome.irri.org/C4rice/).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to a web resource.

claim: Models show that C4 engineering in rice could result in yield increases of 30% to 50%.
source: Models show that increased water and nitrogen use efficiencies from this engineering effort could result in yield increases of 30% to 50% (Karki et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Karki et al., 2013.

claim: Synthetic biology techniques have enabled re-engineering of entire microbial genomes.
source: Synthetic biology techniques have enabled us to re-engineer entire microbial genomes (Hutchison et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hutchison et al., 2016.

claim: Efforts are underway to design synthetic chloroplast genomes.
source: and efforts are underway to design synthetic chloroplast genomes in a similar manner (Scharff and Bock, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Scharff and Bock, 2014.

claim: Gene drives aim to increase the efficiency of existing 'non-drive' methods that employ the concept of reducing population viability.
source: Gene drives are also being considered for restoring ecosystems by, for example, eliminating introduced predators from islands. They aim to increase the efficiency of existing 'non-drive' methods that employ a similar concept of reducing population viability (e.g. by releasing male sterile insects into the environment), but that require repeat treatments.
evidence: This is stated as a description of how gene drives work relative to existing methods.

claim: New innovations are being developed to control the genetic reach of gene drives.
source: Gene drives create risks that might be unpalatable even when balanced against the potential to reduce the number of lives lost to transmittable diseases. New innovations are therefore being developed to control their genetic reach (Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, 2016a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, 2016a.

claim: One approach to controlling gene drives is to include 'kill switches' such as identification markers or in-built susceptibilities to specific treatments.
source: One approach is to include 'kill switches', such as identification markers or in-built susceptibilities to specific treatments or chemicals, which could be used to control the engineered population (Akbari et al., 2015; DiCarlo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Akbari et al., 2015 and DiCarlo et al., 2015.

claim: A 'daisy drive' approach splits gene drive components into smaller, genetically-unlinked units that would eventually segregate in the population, inactivating the drive.
source: A more complex proposition is to intrinsically self-limit the gene drive by deploying it as a 'daisy drive' in which the components of the gene drive are split into smaller, genetically-unlinked units that would eventually segregate in the population, inactivating the drive (Smidler, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Smidler, 2016.

claim: The Broad Institute prohibits its CRISPR technology to be used for gene drives, sterile seeds or tobacco products for human use.
source: For example, the Broad Institute prohibits its CRISPR technology to be used for gene drives, sterile seeds or tobacco products for human use (https://www.broadinstitute.org/news/licensing-crispr-agriculture-policy-considerations).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to a web resource from the Broad Institute.

claim: Many states have taken steps to enable therapeutic genome editing in human somatic cells.
source: Beyond basic research, many states have now taken steps to enable therapeutic genome editing in human somatic cells
evidence: This is stated as a fact about current regulatory developments.

claim: Some states have shown a willingness to directly modify human embryos for medical research.
source: and others have shown a willingness to directly modify human embryos for medical research (Kang et al., 2016a; Liang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kang et al., 2016a and Liang et al., 2015.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 has been shown in human embryos to repair disease-causing mutations.
source: Genome engineering technologies like CRISPR/Cas9 offer the possibility to improve human lifespans and health, recently being shown in human embryos to repair disease-causing mutations (Ma et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ma et al., 2017.

claim: One Chinese leader stated that their government would use all means available to improve the health of the population, including direct genetic modification of its citizens.
source: For example, one Chinese leader previously stated that their government would use all means available to improve the health of the population, including direct genetic modification of its citizens (Carlson, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Carlson, 2012.

claim: DARPA invested $110 million in synthetic biology in 2014.
source: The US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) invested $110 million in synthetic biology in 2014, which accounted for almost 60% of funding for synthetic biology in the US that year
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kuiken, 2015.

claim: DARPA's 2014 investment accounted for almost 60% of funding for synthetic biology in the US that year.
source: The US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) invested $110 million in synthetic biology in 2014, which accounted for almost 60% of funding for synthetic biology in the US that year, and this figure increases to 67% when other Department of Defense funding is included (Kuiken, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kuiken, 2015.

claim: When other Department of Defense funding is included, the figure increases to 67% of US synthetic biology funding in 2014.
source: The US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) invested $110 million in synthetic biology in 2014, which accounted for almost 60% of funding for synthetic biology in the US that year, and this figure increases to 67% when other Department of Defense funding is included (Kuiken, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kuiken, 2015.

claim: The UK Defence Science and Technology Laboratory has invested in synthetic biology, mainly focused on developing novel materials.
source: The UK Defence Science and Technology Laboratory has also invested in synthetic biology, albeit on a smaller scale, and mainly focussed on developing novel materials (DSTL, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to DSTL, 2016.

claim: DARPA's Insect Allies Program intends to use insects to disseminate engineered plant viruses that confer traits to the target plants they feed on.
source: For example, DARPA's Insect Allies Program intends to use insects to disseminate engineered plant viruses that confer traits to the target plants they feed on (Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, 2016b)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, 2016b.

claim: Tissue engineers have built or grown transplantable bladders, hip joints, vaginas, windpipes, veins, arteries, ears, skin, the meniscus of the knee, and patches for damaged hearts.
source: Tissue engineers have already built or grown transplantable bladders, hip joints, vaginas, windpipes, veins, arteries, ears, skin, the meniscus of the knee, and patches for damaged hearts (Ghorbani et al., 2017; Davis et al., 2017; Naito et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ghorbani et al., 2017; Davis et al., 2017; and Naito et al., 2014.

claim: Custom-designed 3D printers can position cells accurately on organ-shaped scaffolds.
source: Would-be organ engineers can now use custom-designed 3D printers to position cells accurately on organ-shaped scaffolds (Wang et al., 2016a)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2016a.

claim: Whole-organ decellularization can create scaffolds ready for implanted cells while preserving the native tissue architecture.
source: Complementing this technology, a technique known as whole-organ decellularization can create scaffolds ready for implanted cells while preserving the native tissue architecture (Peloso et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Peloso et al., 2015.

claim: Living cells printed on to structures have been implanted into animals and have matured into functional tissues.
source: Living cells printed on to structures have been implanted into animals and have matured into functional tissues (Kang et al., 2016b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kang et al., 2016b.

claim: The human microbiome is implicated in Parkinson's disease.
source: The human microbiome is implicated in a large number of human disorders, from Parkinson's to colon cancer (Sampson et al., 2016)

claim: The human microbiome is implicated in colon cancer.
source: The human microbiome is implicated in a large number of human disorders, from Parkinson's to colon cancer (Sampson et al., 2016)

claim: The human microbiome is implicated in metabolic conditions such as obesity and type 2 diabetes.

claim: Synthetic biology approaches could greatly accelerate the development of more effective microbiota-based therapeutics.
source: However, synthetic biology approaches could greatly accelerate the development of more effective microbiota-based therapeutics (Sheth et al., 2016).

claim: Genetically engineered bacterial strains or consortia could be introduced to the host microbiome in cell-based therapies designed to prevent infection, resolve inflammation or treat metabolic disorders.
source: For example, genetically engineered bacterial strains or consortia of natural and engineered microorganisms could be introduced to, or used to supplement, the host microbiome in cell-based therapies designed to prevent infection, resolve inflammation or treat metabolic disorders (Mimee et al., 2016).

claim: Engineered phage-based strategies may prove useful in subtractive therapies aimed at targeting pathogens or shaping host-associated bacterial populations.
source: Engineered phage-based strategies may also prove useful in subtractive therapies aimed at targeting pathogens or shaping host-associated bacterial populations (Citorik et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Citorik et al., 2014.

claim: The majority of influenza vaccines are produced in embryonated chicken eggs in a six-month process.
source: Today, the majority of influenza vaccines are produced in embryonated chicken eggs in a six-month process, before which scientists must predict which strains will be dominant (Milián and Kamen, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Milián and Kamen, 2015.

claim: The 2014/2015 influenza vaccine was announced to be only 23% effective in the USA.
source: In 2014/2015, the vaccine was announced to be only 23% effective in the USA because the dominant virus had been incorrectly predicted and was not included in the vaccine development process (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention et al., 2015).

claim: In 2012, DARPA issued a challenge to produce 10 million doses of the H1N1 flu vaccine within one month of receipt of an emailed genetic sequence.
source: The ability of plant platforms to rapidly respond to large-scale demand and emerging disease threats was first demonstrated in 2012, when DARPA issued a challenge to produce 10 million doses of the H1N1 flu vaccine within one month of receipt of an emailed genetic sequence.
evidence: This is stated as a historical fact about a DARPA challenge.

claim: The Canadian company Medicago successfully responded to DARPA's 2012 vaccine challenge using a wild-relative of tobacco for production.
source: The Canadian company Medicago successfully responded using a wild-relative of tobacco for production (Lomonossoff and D'Aoust, 2016).

claim: Plants can be tailored to produce proteins with human-like post-translational modifications.
source: Plants can now be tailored to produce proteins with human-like post-translational modifications as well as a range of other molecules used as human therapies that are prohibitively expensive or difficult to produce in other systems, widening the range of therapies that could be produced in plants (Li et al., 2016).

claim: Elelyso (Protalix) was approved in 2012 for commercial use in humans to treat Gaucher's disease.

claim: Yeast has been engineered to produce opiates.

claim: Current yields of opiates from engineered yeast are insufficient for the isolation of significant quantities of products.
source: Although yields are currently insufficient for the isolation of significant quantities of products (Endy et al., 2015)

claim: An Escherichia coli genome has been modified to no longer use one of the 64 codons normally recognised in protein synthesis.
source: An Escherichia coli genome has been modified to no longer use one of the 64 codons normally recognised in protein synthesis: the cells containing this genome can instead use this free codon to programmably insert non-standard amino acids with alternative physical and chemical properties into proteins, while still translating the original protein repertoire required for growth (Lajoie et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lajoie et al., 2013.

claim: Recoded E. coli cells can use a free codon to programmably insert non-standard amino acids into proteins while still translating the original protein repertoire required for growth.

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lajoie et al., 2013.

claim: Recoded cells can be made dependent on the supply of a non-standard amino acid for survival by encoding its incorporation into essential genes.
source: However, recoded cells can be limited to controlled conditions: by encoding the incorporation of a non-standard amino acid into essential genes, the cell is dependent on the supply of this amino acid for survival and will die in any environment where this is not provided (Mandell et al., 2015; Rovner et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mandell et al., 2015 and Rovner et al., 2015.

claim: Automated fabrication with biological materials is establishing itself in the form of services provided by 'biofactories' in universities and companies.
source: Automated fabrication with biological materials and the subsequent characterization of engineered materials and cells is now establishing itself in the form of services provided by 'biofactories' in a number of universities and companies (Check Hayden, 2014).

claim: It is now possible to travel with a hand-held sequencer and go from sample to sequence in less than 24 hours.
source: Moreover, it is now possible to travel with a hand-held sequencer and to go from sample to sequence in less than 24 hours (Quick et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Quick et al., 2016.

claim: Ten million doses of vaccine were produced just a month after receipt of an email containing the sequence of the viral strain.
source: The enormous benefits of this rapid online transmission and synthesis of genetic information are already being realized, for example, through the production of ten million doses of vaccine just a month after receipt of an email containing the sequence of the viral strain (Powell, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Powell, 2015.

claim: Researchers from the University of Washington successfully engineered a DNA sequence to exploit a vulnerability they introduced into DNA sequencing software.
source: The latter scenario was recently simulated by researchers from the University of Washington, who successfully engineered a DNA sequence to exploit a vulnerability they introduced into DNA sequencing software (Ney, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ney, 2017.

claim: The Nagoya Protocol entered into force in 2014.

evidence: This is stated as a fact about the protocol's implementation date.

claim: 93 countries are signatory to the Nagoya Protocol at the time of writing.
source: It is expected to change the way genetic materials are treated by countries that are signatory to the protocol (93 at the time of writing).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the number of signatories.

claim: 'Digital Sequence Information of Genetic Resources' was discussed at a CBD meeting in December 2016 (the COP13 meeting).
source: 'Digital Sequence Information of Genetic Resources' was discussed at a CBD meeting in December 2016 (the COP13 meeting) and recognised to be a cross-cutting issue (Convention on Biological Diversity, 2016).

claim: One of six Chinese nationals charged by the US Government pleaded guilty for attempting to steal trade secrets from GM seed companies.

claim: Biosynthetic pathways for hydrocodone have been re-engineered into yeast.

claim: Biosynthetic pathways for artemisinin have been re-engineered into yeast.

claim: In 2015, a biohacking team in Oakland, California, secured crowd-funding to develop an open source protocol for making inexpensive generic insulin from E. coli.
source: For example, in 2015, a biohacking team in Oakland, California, secured crowd-funding to develop an open source protocol for making inexpensive generic insulin from E. coli (Stelzer, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stelzer, 2016.

claim: Standardized influenza vaccine backbones enable rapid development of vaccine candidates.
source: Existing examples include standardized influenza vaccine backbones for the rapid development of vaccine candidates (Dormitzer et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dormitzer et al., 2013.

claim: Plant-based antibody production systems exist.
source: and plant-based antibody production systems (Olinger et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Olinger et al., 2012.

claim: Most strains of Bacillus cereus are harmless.
source: For example, most strains of Bacillus cereus are harmless, but the identification of toxigenic strains (Okinaka et al., 2006) has prompted the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to rewrite rules and include this strain as a select agent (US Department of Health and Human Services, 2016).

claim: The identification of toxigenic strains of Bacillus cereus prompted the US CDC to rewrite rules and include this strain as a select agent.
source: For example, most strains of Bacillus cereus are harmless, but the identification of toxigenic strains (Okinaka et al., 2006) has prompted the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to rewrite rules and include this strain as a select agent (US Department of Health and Human Services, 2016).

claim: The UK Synthetic Biology Leadership Council Strategic Plan targets a £10 billion synthetic biology based platform in the UK by 2030.

claim: In the latest horizon scan for issues likely to impact the future of global conservation and the environment, four of the 15 prioritised topics were biotechnology applications.
source: In the latest horizon scan for issues likely to impact the future of global conservation and the environment (Sutherland et al., 2017), four of the 15 prioritised topics were biotechnology applications: creating fuel from bionic leaves; reverse photosynthesis for biofuel production; manipulating coral symbionts to avoid mass coral bleaching; and extensive use of bacteria and fungi to manage agricultural pests and diseases.

claim: In a recent vote in Florida, 57% of voters across Monroe county supported the release of genetically engineered mosquitoes to combat mosquito borne diseases.
